chapter: The Search for Dulcinea and Her Transformation (to p. 106), then the opening of The Strange Knight and Squire

facts: Chapter 8 opens, titled The Search for Dulcinea, Her Transformation, and the Masked Players
The knight rode his brave Rocinante and Sancho his trusty Dapple, with pouches well-supplied and their purses full of money
They set their course for Toboso, the home of the imaginary Lady Dulcinea
Don Quixote gave his reason for going there first: he must have all the blessings of her ladyship in order to have good fortune in the perilous adventures that await them
Sancho answered that it will be difficult to see her alone, or get her blessing, unless she tosses it over the fence of the yard where he saw her last time
Don Quixote said it was impossible that it was a fence, and that Sancho must mean the galleries, the arcades of a rich and royal palace
Sancho replied that what he saw was a fence, if his eyesight and memory are worth anything

Don Quixote said they shall go there, for whether there be chinks or lattices, one flash from the bright sun of her beauty will inflame his soul and fortify his heart so that no one will be able to compete with him in skill or courage
Sancho said he did not see any flashes, but that might be because the dust of the winnowing made a cloud around her face
The next day they came in sight of Toboso without meeting any adventure
Deciding not to enter the town before nightfall, they rested in the shade of some oak trees near the road
It was much later when they got into the city and all the inhabitants seemed to be in bed
Except for the barking of dogs, the whole town was hushed in silence
Don Quixote told Sancho to lead on to the palace, for it is possible she is still awake
Sancho asked what palace, saying it was a small, ordinary house when he saw it
Don Quixote said that was no doubt some pavilion attached to the castle, where the great ladies retire for amusement
Sancho said this is not the time to be rousing people from their beds, anyhow
Don Quixote said they should first find the castle and then decide what to do, and pointed out a vast building that must be his lady's palace
Sancho said that is clearly a church, and that he had already told his worship the lady lives down an alley
The knight cried Blockhead, and asked whether palaces exist on alleys
Sancho answered that he knows not, that every country has its own customs, and that it may be the fashion there to build palaces on alleys and backyards
They asked a passing laborer about Lady Dulcinea, but he knew nothing
As day was beginning to break, Sancho suggested that they retire into some woods near town to rest, and that later on he would come alone and search for her ladyship's house
The knight agreed and they rode a couple of miles out of town, where they found shelter in a shady grove
It was still early in the day when Sancho emerged from the grove, pretending to go find Dulcinea and puzzled about how he would get around his master on this matter
Sancho went a little way and then turned off the road, intending to hide until evening so that Don Quixote would think he was occupied with his mission into Toboso
He sat and thought for a long time and had not come to any conclusion
Just as he was about to return to his master, he saw three peasant girls mounted on donkeys coming from the direction of the city
He had been thinking that if only he could get hold of some country girl, he could persuade his master that she was Lady Dulcinea in disguise, and here came the very thing he wanted
So, riding back to where Don Quixote sat, he called out to him to mount at once and ride into the road, for here comes Lady Dulcinea and two of her damsels to pay him a visit
Don Quixote exclaimed Gracious Heaven and asked whether Sancho was not deceived, or was deceiving him
Sancho answered not a bit, and told him to see for himself
He described the princess and her attendants as blazing all over with gold and diamonds and pearls and rubies, with their hair flying behind their shoulders like bundles of sunbeams
He said they were mounted on the three finest belfrys he ever saw
Don Quixote corrected him: palfreys, Sancho
Sancho said belfrys or palfreys, it is all the same for what it matters
Sancho finished praising them as the finest ladies he ever set eyes on, especially Princess Dulcinea, who is perfectly dazzling
As Sancho and Don Quixote emerged from the wood, Sancho whispered that there they are, shining like the sun
Don Quixote said he saw only three plain-looking country girls riding on donkeys
Sancho, pretending to be amazed, asked whether it was possible he saw only donkeys where there are three belfrys, as white as pure snow
Don Quixote insisted they are donkeys, or at least they appear so to him
Sancho solemnly told him to say no more, but clear his eyes if he can and come pay reverence to the mistress of his soul, even if she be in a disguise
Then he led the way to where the girls were passing, took hold of the bridle of one donkey, and fell to his knees in the dust

He addressed the girl as Queen, Princess, Duchess of Beauty, asking her grandness to be pleased to receive the homage of yon captive knight, who stands there turned to stone by her amazing beauty and magnificent presence
He began to introduce himself as Sancho Panza

glossary.palfrey: A light saddle horse suitable for a woman to ride.

facts: A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with Sancho taking hold of the donkey's bridle and falling to his knees
Sancho finished his introduction: he is the squire, and his master is Don Quixote de la Mancha, otherwise known as the Knight of the Sorrowful Face
By this time Don Quixote was also on his knees in front of the girl
But he could see only her wide, homely face and flat nose
He felt so confused that he could not say a word
For their part, the girls were astonished and bewildered both at being stopped and at being addressed in such a fashion
The one who had been called Queen first broke the silence
The girl told them to get out of the way, calling them a couple of fools, and to let the girls go about their business
Sancho began again, addressing her as Princess and universal lady of Toboso, but stopped when another girl blurted out at him to shut up, calling him an idiot
She said it is a pretty thing that three poor girls cannot go along a public road without nincompoops like him and that other fellow trying to make fun of them
Don Quixote sadly whispered to Sancho to rise, saying he sees now that fate has shot her last cruel arrow into his wretched heart
He said the enchanters have doomed him never to see the matchless Lady Dulcinea in her own person
He said they have degraded her beauty into the coarse looks of a country girl, and may even turn her into a goblin just to increase his suffering
Nevertheless he turned to one of the girls and asked her to bestow on him one loving look, one kind word
The girl said Oh bother, told him to talk his gibberish somewhere else, and to leave them alone
They put their donkeys in motion and trotted quickly away
They had not got far when the donkey of the one Don Quixote had imagined to be Lady Dulcinea began to kick and buck so that the girl was thrown to the ground
Sancho and Don Quixote ran to help her, but she was on her legs before they could do much
She ran toward her donkey, whose back was to her, vaulted into the saddle like a man and rode off laughing with her companions
Sancho exclaimed By St. Roque that their Lady Dulcinea is as agile as a bird and fit to ride against any jockey in Spain or Mexico
Don Quixote watched the retreating figure and said sadly that Sancho now sees how he is persecuted
He said the evil enchanters will not let him have the pleasure of seeing his lady as she really is
He said they make her condition as unattractive to him as possible
He said that instead of the fragrant scent she has from living among flowers, they give her the smell of garlic, which he distinctly noticed
Sancho agreed they are vile creatures and said he should like to see them all strung up by the gills like smoked fish
He said they might at least have left her breath alone
He added that all the same she seemed to him all sweetness and beauty, and that she had on her lip a lovely mole with seven or eight splendid hairs growing out of it like threads of gold

glossary.St. Roque: Also Roch. A saint, born in France, who gave to the poor the vast riches he inherited and then travelled the roads in a pilgrim's garb, nursing victims of the plague from city to city in Italy. He is a patron saint of prisoners and the sick.

facts: Don Quixote remarked that those were rather long hairs for a mole
Sancho assured him they were there
Don Quixote said no doubt, and that if she had a hundred they would all be additions to her beauty, like so many bright stars
He said woe is me who is unable to see any of this, and that surely he is the most unfortunate of men
Sancho struggled to keep from laughing at the success of his trick
After some more conversation of the same sort, they mounted their beasts and took the road to Saragossa, where a great annual festival was about to take place
Chapter 8 ends here
Chapter 9 opens, titled The Strange Knight and Squire, Challenge, Victory and Transformation
Master and man laid themselves down to pass the night under some wide-spreading oak trees
Sancho slept soundly, but before long Don Quixote's lighter slumber was disturbed by the sound of voices
Sitting up, he saw two men on horseback
He heard one say to the other to stop and attend to the horses, for the place seemed to offer not only pasture but the silence and solitude his thoughts of love require
With that the speaker dismounted and stretched out on the grass with such a rattling of armor that it caught Don Quixote's attention
Don Quixote thought the man must be a knight-errant like himself
So he crept over to Sancho and whispered for him to wake up, because here was an adventure
The drowsy squire answered that he prayed to heaven it would be a safe and profitable one
Don Quixote explained what he had seen and heard, and just then the sound of a guitar reached them
Sancho said it certainly must be some knight or other in love
Don Quixote said all knight-errants are in love
Then the mysterious knight began singing a love song, not very well, nor was his guitar-playing good
When he finished he sighed deeply and addressed the most beautiful and cruel of women, divine Casildea de Vandalia, asking whether her tormented knight is to waste away in wandering and toil
He asked whether it is not enough that he has caused her superior beauty to be admitted by all the knights of Navarre, Leon, Castile, and all the knights of La Mancha
Don Quixote said to Sancho that this is not true, for he is a knight of La Mancha and he has never made such an acknowledgement, nor will he ever make one so unfavorable to his lady
He concluded that the stranger is raving
The strange knight, hearing voices, called out to ask who is there, and whether they are among the happy or the sad
Don Quixote answered: the sad
A half-page engraving sits at the top, captioned with the stranger's squire drawing Sancho aside
The stranger told Don Quixote to come there, then, and behold the very model of sorrow and misery
The mournful stranger took Don Quixote by the arm and invited him to sit down
Don Quixote said that from what he had just heard, he took it the stranger's woes are due to love, an unrequited passion for a fair lady
The stranger nodded, and asked if Don Quixote was also suffering so
Don Quixote replied that this is his fate, though he cannot exactly say his lady scorns him
Sancho put in that certainly she does not, for she is as gentle as a lamb and as soft as butter
The stranger demanded whether this is his squire, and whether he allows him to speak when his master is in a conversation
Sancho said he can talk and has talked to better people than the stranger, but never mind, the less said the sooner mended
The stranger's squire now drew Sancho aside, saying come, let us chat together, and let our masters talk as they please about their love problems
Away they went to discuss the hardships squires put up with
The stranger's squire said the hope of reward makes up for a lot, and that it is a poor knight-errant who cannot bestow an earldom, or a government, on his squire
Sancho answered that his master has promised him the governorship of an island
The stranger's squire said his own master is offering him a fat canonry
Sancho said that then his master is a knight of the church, in some sort
Sancho said his own master was advised to be an archbishop, but he would be nothing less than the emperor
He said he is always afraid his master will turn to the church and leave him in the lurch, for he has no learning that way

glossary.canonry: A priest on the staff of a cathedral or in a religious community.

facts: The other squire said Sancho may find that island government is more trouble than profit
He said that likely enough, if they were wise men they would stay at home with their families instead of tramping around the country
He described his own master as one who is as crazy as he is brave, and even more than that, is a scoundrel
Sancho answered that his own master is certainly mad, but he is not a liar
He said his master is as honest and innocent as a babe, and that you can persuade him of anything
He said that is why he loves him and cannot leave him in spite of all his follies
The other said it is the blind leading the blind and they will all end up in a ditch
He said talking is making him dry, and that he has something in his saddlebag that will moisten their tongues
As he said it he pulled out a flask of wine and a large rabbit pie
Both men went on eating, drinking, and talking until at last they fell asleep
Meanwhile their masters spent the time in courteous knightly conversation
The other knight was saying that he fell desperately in love with Casildea de Vandalia, and that she tested his devotion by laying tasks on him

glossary.archbishop: The head of a province in the Roman Catholic Church.
